title: AAL (Agent Access Layer)
pitch: WebMCP gives agents tools. AAL adds identity, user-authorized permissions, spending limits, approvals, and verifiable receipts to WebMCP for consequential actions.
about_excerpt: WebMCP gives agents tools. AAL adds identity, user-authorized permissions, spending limits, approvals, and verifiable receipts to WebMCP for consequential actions. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration WebMCP gives AI agents a much better way to interact with the web. Instead of looking at pixels, finding buttons, and simulating clicks, an agent can discover structured tools that a website exposes directly: search_products() add_to_cart() place_order() change_subscription() That felt like a major shift. But it also exposed a missing layer. If a website gives an agent place_order() , who says the agent is allowed to call it? WebMCP provides the interface between a website and an agent, but consequential actions introduce a different set of questions: Which user is the agent acting for? Which tools did that user authorize? How much can the agent spend? How long does that authority last? Which actions still require human approval? What happens if execution fails halfway through? Can we prove what was actually authorized and executed? We built AAL — Agent Access Layer to answer those questions. The simplest way we describe it is: WebMCP gives agents tools. AAL gives them permission to use them. What it does AAL adds a delegation and transaction layer around WebMCP. A user can connect an agent to a website and grant it explicit authority: which WebMCP tools it can call, under what limits, and which actions require additional approval. For a simple read, the agent can call the tool normally. For a consequential action, AAL turns the call into a transaction: Agent calls WebMCP tool ↓ Site prepares exact action ↓ AAL checks permissions + limits ↓ User or policy approves ↓ Site commits the action ↓ Signed receipt Under the hood, AAL focuses on four things: Delegation — explicit grants connect a user, a site, an agent session, a set of tools, and bounded permissions. Authorization — consequential WebMCP calls use a prepare → approve → commit flow instead of allowing page JavaScript to directly trigger effects. Accountability — grants, commitments, approvals, and outcomes are linked together with signed, verifiable receipts. Metering — agent activity can be measured using evidence tied to the authorized call, creating a path toward websites charging agents or agent platforms for usage. We also built an AAL SDK so this isn't limited to our demo. A developer building a WebMCP-powered site can integrate AAL into their existing tools and add delegation, permissions, approvals, limits, and receipts without rebuilding the protocol from scratch. The goal is for a developer to go from: WebMCP tool to: WebMCP tool + AAL policy = authorized agent capability For the demo, we pushed this all the way through a payment flow using WebMCP + AAL + x402 + Base Sepolia test USDC . The agent can construct a transaction, but it cannot approve its own consequential action. The user sees the exact payment terms, explicitly approves them, the designated wallet authorizes the payment, and the resulting execution can be reconciled into a verifiable receipt. How we built it We intentionally treated WebMCP as the tool transport , not the security boundary. AAL is built around three core pieces, packaged behind an SDK that WebMCP developers can integrate into their own sites. AAL SDK The SDK is the developer-facing layer. It gives WebMCP-powered sites a straightforward way to: register tools with AAL declare which tools are read-only or consequential define permissions and limits connect server-side prepare and commit handlers add agent delegation trigger approval when required handle revocation and session state return signed transaction receipts The goal was to hide as much protocol complexity as possible while keeping the important security boundaries intact. Developers should be able to keep building normal WebMCP tools while AAL handles the authorization lifecycle around them. WebMCP adapter A lightweight browser adapter detects WebMCP and exposes the site's tools to the agent. It handles the agent-facing interaction, consent UX, approvals, pending states, and receipt presentation. But it intentionally has very little authority. It cannot decide that an agent is authorized to spend money, mutate application state, or bypass a policy. Site transaction service The site's backend is the actual enforcement point. It: authenticates the site's user validates the WebMCP tool against a server-owned catalog verifies the agent's grant enforces tool and spending limits prepares the exact proposed effect reserves authorization capacity verifies required approval executes server-side handlers records the resulting state signs receipts One of our most important rules is: Page JavaScript never gets to decide that an agent is authorized to perform a consequential action. Grant Service The Grant Service handles explicit delegation. The user approves a grant covering a specific site, specific WebMCP tools, limits, expiration, and required forms of evidence. The site keeps the actual grant and enforcement logic server-side; the browser receives only the information necessary to drive the experience. We built the protocol around deterministic schemas, signatures, canonical hashes, idempotency keys, state machines, revocation, and conformance vectors so authorization decisions can be reproduced instead of depending on implementation-specific behavior. For the x402 demo, we added a separate trusted approval surface and a deliberately constrained testnet payment flow so we could test AAL against a real consequential action rather than just a toy API call. Challenges we ran into WebMCP exposes capability, not authority The first challenge was architectural. A WebMCP tool being available does not mean an agent should automatically be allowed to use it. We had to separate: "This tool exists" from: "This agent is authorized to use this tool, for this user, under these conditions." That distinction shaped the entire project. Making the protocol easy enough to actually integrate Designing a secure authorization protocol is one problem. Making it something a normal WebMCP developer would actually use is another. AAL has grants, commitments, proofs, approvals, receipts, revocation, limits, and recovery state. We didn't want every website developer to have to understand or implement all of that themselves. That is why the SDK became such an important part of the project. The challenge was finding the right abstraction: hide the protocol machinery without hiding the security model . A developer should mostly think about their tool, its effects, and the policy around it. AAL should handle the rest. Browser JavaScript is not trustworthy enough It would have been much easier to implement authorization in the page itself. But an XSS vulnerability, compromised dependency, or malicious page script could then alter tool descriptions, transaction terms, or approval flows. live_observation.first_impression: Northline Outfitters is a fashion storefront centered on an AI Stylist prompt, with a prefilled outfit request and many outfit-item controls.
live_observation.action_attempted: Clicked “STYLE MY OUTFIT” for the prefilled blue-jeans and cropped-white-T-shirt request.
live_observation.after_state: The styling action completed on the storefront without requiring personal data or sign-in; the resulting state was not detailed in the accessibility snapshot.
live_observation.notes: The storefront clearly demonstrates an agent-facing styling action, but spending limits, approvals, identity, and receipts were not directly exercised.
